questions.prompt: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
questions.explanation: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four 8-bit octets (0–255). IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.

questions.prompt: Which of these are private (RFC 1918) IPv4 addresses? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.0.0/16, and 172.16.0.0/12 (172.16–172.31) are private. 203.0.113.9 is in a public documentation range, not private.

questions.prompt: In an IPv6 address, a single run of all-zero groups can be replaced by the symbol ____ (used at most once).
questions.explanation: '::' compresses one contiguous run of all-zero 16-bit groups, and may appear only once per address to stay unambiguous.

questions.prompt: Match each address to its category.
questions.explanation: 127.0.0.1 is loopback, 192.168.x.x is private, 169.254.x.x is link-local, and 8.8.8.8 is a public address.

questions.prompt: Which statement about IPv6 is correct?

options.text: It is 128 bits and has no broadcast address (uses multicast/anycast)
It is 64 bits and uses the same broadcast as IPv4
It is written in dotted decimal like IPv4
The '::' shortcut can be used as many times as you like

questions.explanation: IPv6 is 128 bits, written in hex groups, has no broadcast (multicast/anycast instead), and '::' may be used only once.
First drop leading zeros in each group, then replace the single run of all-zero groups with '::'.
